title: Citizens (1791)
carry: a door opened, with a price

lines: A LINE ABOUT TO BE ERASED?
cards: A hall in Paris, crowded and loud. The French Revolution has torn up the old order, and the new assembly has declared that men are born free and equal in rights.
Now a hard question is on the floor: does that include the Jews? Some deputies say yes, obviously. Others say Jews are a separate nation and can never be truly French.
The debate goes back and forth, session after session. A people who have lived behind lines drawn by others wait to hear whether a line is about to be erased. Today, one word: citizens.

teach.b: The answer, in the end, was yes. Revolutionary France made Jews full citizens, with the same rights as anyone else: to live where they chose, to work in any trade, to vote. For Jews in France, it changed daily life.
But it came with a bargain, and one deputy, Count Stanislas de Clermont-Tonnerre, put it bluntly.
Roughly: to the Jews as a nation, nothing; to the Jews as individuals, everything. You may be equal, one by one, but not as a community that governs itself.

Remember the Council of Four Lands, and the Jewish courts and councils that had run Jewish life? Citizenship asked Jews to hand much of that to the state, and become French citizens of the Jewish faith.
Some welcomed that as freedom at last. Others worried about what a people loses when it becomes only a religion.
The Torah has its own line about equal law, though there it is a command to Israel about the stranger among them.
In Leviticus, the King James Bible reads: "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for one of your own country." In Europe, Jews had long been the strangers.
Now a country offered them one manner of law.

teach.h: A DOOR OPENED, WITH A PRICE.
teach.b: That closes a week of boundaries: Volozhin, the Pale, the cantonists, Salanter, Mendelssohn and the maskilim, and now a vote that opened a door, with a price attached.

how: Traditional Jewish prayer books include a prayer for the welfare of the government, said in the Shabbat service.

games.q: you're a deputy in the assembly. a colleague says Jews are a separate nation and can never be French. what did the assembly finally do?
o: make Jews full citizens, as individuals.
make Jews citizens only in Paris.
games.why: Jews became full citizens, equal in rights, as individuals rather than as a self-governing community.

practice: Think of one right you have where you live that you rarely think about: to vote, to move, to speak, to worship or not to worship; if you're not a citizen there, think of one protection you do have.
Let it become concrete, and remember the people in that Paris hall, waiting to hear whether that right was theirs. If you pray, you can give thanks for it in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Citizens. Revolutionary France made Jews full and equal citizens, as individuals, asking them to become French citizens of the Jewish faith. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a door opened, with a price. Equal as individuals, not as a nation. That's the week.
